Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I have to be on guard all the time

issues.explanation: 'Shouting in Arabic' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless there is specific trauma detail indicating the stalker used Arabic; with the rest of the profile, this trigger appears overly specific and disconnected from the other stalking-related items.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the same Memory node items describing fragmented, intrusive, partially inaccessible trauma memory ('extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'fragments appear suddenly without warning'). While not impossible, this is a direct enough tension within the node to question coherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: Fear of losing control of anger and doing something terrible is poorly integrated with the rest of the profile, which centers on fear, mistrust, stranger threat, and life damage after stalking. It points toward a perpetration/harm-to-others concern not otherwise represented in Threat, Triggers, Memory, or strategies, making the formulation less coherent.

vignette: Clara was twenty-two when the man began appearing outside her apartment. It started with a figure standing under the streetlamp across from her building, then progressed to the sound of boots on her fire escape. She remembered one night with devastating precision: the heavy, ragged breathing echoing in the stairwell as he climbed toward her door, the paper sliding under her frame, the way her own pulse had hammered against her ribs until she called the police. After the officers arrived and documented the threats, the case went cold. The man vanished, but his absence did not bring relief. Instead, Clara found herself standing in the school parking lot every morning, scanning the perimeter before stepping toward her classroom. At twenty-eight, teaching seventh-grade history in a suburban district, she had come to believe that people simply could not be trusted, that the safety she had once taken for granted was gone forever. Her classroom had become a place of quiet dread. What frightened her most was the sudden silence that followed the final bell, a quiet that made her certain something dangerous was about to happen. She would keep her desk lamp on until her partner called, certain that the stillness was a prelude to intrusion. Strangers approaching her in the grocery aisle or waiting in line at the café sent spikes of fear, horror, and shame through her body; she had stopped looking up from her phone, bracing for a touch or a word that might turn into pursuit. When a parent’s husband approached her to discuss a grading dispute, Clara’s hands shook and she stepped back until another teacher intervened, her mind flooded with the same dread that had gripped her that night in the stairwell. She told herself she had to be on guard all the time, that lowering her shoulders for even a moment would be catastrophic. The school corridors, once familiar, now felt like potential paths of pursuit, and she mapped her days around the belief that she was constantly being followed or tracked. The memories of what happened refused to settle into a coherent story. Some fragments arrived unbidden: the exact pattern of frost on the windowpane that night, the scuff mark on the man’s boot, the way her own voice had cracked when she begged him to leave. Then those details would vanish, leaving only hollow gaps where she knew what had occurred but could not find words to describe it. When her partner asked her to recount the stalking, she would sit at the kitchen table, jaw tight, knowing the event had destroyed her life yet unable to string the pieces together for him. Heavy breathing from a passing delivery driver or the sound of a neighbor’s shower running set off a full-body flinch; she would step back, eyes darting to the exit, certain she was being tracked again. The sight of marked patrol cars rolling down her street would lock her breath, her mind flashing to the officers who had once come to help, now reading as another kind of threat. Over the past eight months, Clara’s avoidance had accumulated like snow. She took different routes to school, arrived hours before her first class, and declined every invitation to visit friends after dark. Her lesson plans grew rigid; she avoided the staff lounge where conversations might spill into unguarded tones, retreating to the empty library instead. She moved through her days in a state of constant readiness, and the emotional toll had drained the color from her world. She had come to believe her life was ruined, that the woman who used to laugh without checking the locks no longer existed. When her partner gently suggested she speak to someone about the exhaustion etched into her posture, Clara finally agreed. What she most feared was that no one would understand how close the danger still felt, and what she most hoped for was a way to quiet the alarms in her head long enough to simply walk down the street without looking over her shoulder.
